It's more complicated and arguably worse than that.

Back before the great depression retail banks were largely a local affair. Bank managers knew everyone and knew everyone's business, which empowered them to make good decisions when lending money. You would pay money into a savings account, the bank manager would lend it out to safe local investments which he knew intimitely, then when you retired there was plenty of interest payments to cover your pension.

Then the great depression hit. Suddenly no one could pay back their loans, no matter how cautious the bank manager had been, because so many businesses were failing. Even after the worst of the crash had passed, banks were being extremely cautious and only lending to the safest borrowers. As a result, young couples starting out in life often couldn't get a mortgage.

President Roosevelt set out to solve the problem as part of his new deal. If the banks made mortgages that satisfied certain conditions, they could sell the mortgage to a federal agency (Federal National Mortgage Association or Fannie Mae) and get all of their money back immediately. This achieved three things:

  • It removed the risk assessment function of local bankers, and instead transferred it to politicians. The ones deciding if a borrower could actually pay the loan back were no longer local figures who intimately knew the community, they were civil servants and elected representatives hundreds or thousands of miles away who had never met the people involved.

  • It effectively granted the federal government urban planning authority over the entire country: They could simply set the conditions of these free loans to require any planning goals they wished. Prior to fannie mae, banks had mostly lent to mixed use properties in urban areas. With commercial space at street level and residential space above. Post fannie mae, they were required to lend to mostly suburban developments outside the cities to create demand for automobiles and mass transit.

  • Banks main job went from being risk assessment, to compliance. Instead of having to compete by knowing their community better than other banks, they competed by lobbying for regulations that suited their business model better and by filling out federal paperwork. This lead to the agglutination of banks into megacorps and the disappearance of local branches.

Naturally this system was doomed to failure from the start. In the boom years following WW2, where the US had no industrial competition it was propped up (along with any number of other wasteful policies) by the fact that the US had a captive market. Once that changed in the 70s and 80s things started to go screwy.

Remember how I said politicians were now in the risk assessment business? Name me a politician that's willing to tell a poor person he can't have a mansion because he can't afford it. There are only a handful of such people. and none of them have ever been president. So president after president relaxed the standards needed to qualify for free loans, and gradually retail banks were instructed to lend more and more to people with less and less.

Eventually this came to a head during the financial crash and sank the economy for a few years. We all heard how the crash was caused by "greedy bankers" which is true. But what we're not told is that the greedy bankers were directly instructed to be greedy and make unsafe loans, and that this process was made possible by new-deal laws.

You're referring to NINJA loans - No Income, No Job (and no) Assets. The "Can you fog a mirror" loan - these were literally given to anyone regardless of their ability to pay it back. In my area, instant refinance companies popped up everywhere, and money was easy to get. Banks had people standing in drive-through lanes handing out mortgage and equity loan applications. These were "bad" loans.

The real problem was banks were now allowed to produce their own investment vehicles, the Glass-Stegall act (a Depression-era inspired piece of legislation that prevented commercial banks - your deposit accounts - from being an investment bank like Lehman Brothers) having been repealed in 1999. Banks immediately started to package these loans up in investment vehicles and offering them as derivatives (betting on the outcome of the loans, but not the loans themselves) and offering the loans in tranches (levels) of risk as investments themselves, aided by the ratings firms who gave these turds good ratings.

As the housing crash started in earnest, the people that had no jobs or assets couldn't pay the loans back. The term "Jingle Mail" - the act of sending the keys to the financier - became a common term. As the loans failed, these terrible investments that should have been rated terrible started to fail, and the investment banks that promoted them (along with mortgagers) started to collapse. Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, Countrywide...commercial banks that were hit with the bad loans started to fail, National City Bank (of Cleveland) being one, along with a lot of regionals and locals that got on the loan bandwagon.

Other companies, like Blackrock (who presided over the largest corporate mortgage failure to that date) stood by staunchly saying "We believe this is the bottom and it's ok now" as more and more investment and commercial banks failed.

The fallout having happened, a lot of investment and commercial banks failed and were force-bought by other banks, or simply died and were absorbed by other institutions. Dodd-Frank, which re-placed a lot of laws from G-S, came into being. This is where we are now, banks are showing signs of trying the same shit as before but are somewhat limited by Dodd-Frank.
